--- Page 1 ---
Scalable Placement for Disaggregated LLM Serving
on Heterogeneous Edge Fleets
Truong-Thanh Le†, Hoang-Loc La§, Amir Taherkordi†, Frank Eliassen† and Phuong Hoai Ha§
† Department of Informatics
University of Oslo
Oslo, Norway
{truongl,amirhost,frank}@ifi.uio.no
§ Department of Computer Science
UiT The Arctic University of Norway
Tromsø, Norway
{hoang.l.la,phuong.hoai.ha}@uit.no
Abstract—Serving large language models (LLMs) at the edge is
increasingly desirable for privacy-sensitive applications and sce-
narios that require data to remain on local devices. However, edge
environments are constrained by limited computational resources
and exhibit substantial device heterogeneity, making efficient
LLM serving challenging. These limitations become particularly
pronounced under bursty demand, where congestion and queue
buildup can significantly increase response latency. Replicating
the model into multiple pipeline instances can improve serving
capacity and reduce congestion. Yet, deciding how devices should
be grouped into replicas, assigning replicas to prefill or decode
functions, and partitioning model layers across heterogeneous de-
vices jointly creates a large combinatorial optimization problem.
We present SPADE, a scalable and runtime-efficient placement
planner for disaggregated LLM serving with pipeline replica-
tion across heterogeneous edge clusters. SPADE introduces a
dominance-based pruning technique that discards inferior replica
candidates and recursively eliminates larger candidates that
contain them, dramatically shrinking the search space. It further
combines a water-filling approach for layer partitioning with a
bounded multidimensional knapsack formulation that optimizes
placement under a congestion-aware objective. On a synthetic
fleet of 30 devices spanning five hardware classes, SPADE finds
the optimal placement in 441 ms. In contrast, a genetic-search
baseline augmented with dynamic-programming partitioning re-
quires approximately two hours and still produces solutions with
a 19.7% worse congestion objective. When evaluated on fleets
containing ten device types, SPADE’s pruning strategy eliminates
99.6% of candidate placements while yielding the same surviving
candidate set as exhaustive enumeration.
Index Terms—Scalable placement planner, search space prun-
ing, disaggregated LLM serving, queueing system
I. INTRODUCTION
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly moving
from centralized datacenters to edge deployments [1], driven
by privacy requirements that prevent organizations and indi-
vidual users from sending sensitive data to third-party APIs
[2]. Instead of running on homogeneous clusters, these de-
ployments must operate on the available hardware [3, 4, 5]
connected through commodity local-area networks rather than
high-speed interconnects such as NVLink. Hence, the execu-
tion environment is inherently heterogeneous in architecture,
memory capacity, and communication bandwidth [6, 7, 8].
Deploying modern LLMs on such fleets is challenging
because model sizes, activations and KV cache usage often
exceed the memory capacity of any single device [3, 5]. Mem-
ory therefore is one of the main factors that determines both
where the model can be placed and how many requests can
be served concurrently [9]. Consequently, pipeline parallelism
is the fundamental mechanism that enables LLM serving in
the first place [10, 11, 12]. Moreover, LLM serving is itself
heterogeneous. Prefill is compute-intensive and processes an
entire prompt at once, whereas Decode is memory-intensive
and generates tokens iteratively. This heterogeneity motivates
LLM disaggregation in datacenter systems [13, 14]. At the
edge, disaggregation becomes even more challenging because
the available devices differ substantially.
An edge fleet must also serve many concurrent requests
with limited compute and memory capacity, so requests can
readily arrive faster than it can process them; time-to-first-
token (TTFT) then becomes dominated by congestion, the time
requests spend waiting in queues [15]. Deploying multiple
pipeline replicas, each a complete copy of the LLM deployed
across a subset of devices, alleviates congestion but turns de-
ployment into a placement problem: devices must be allocated
across model replicas, each model replica assigned to Prefill or
Decode, and layers partitioned across each replica’s devices.
Existing solutions address only parts of this problem. Halda [3]
and LOIP [5] optimize single-pipeline deployments for single-
request latency, while Helix [6] and Parallax [4] maximize
aggregate throughput without Prefill–Decode role assignment.
E2LLM [9] is closest to our work, targeting congestion with
Prefill and Decode replicas; however, its objective combines
Prefill service time with congestion, which can favor Prefill
capacity even when it does not shorten queues, and its ge-
netic search provides no optimality guarantee. What remains
missing is an objective that isolates congestion, together with
a search that finds the optimal placement at fleet scale.
Finding this optimum is hard because placement nests two
problems. The outer problem allocates devices to replicas and
assigns each replica a phase; it is NP-hard [16, 17], with up
to 2N candidate replicas for N devices. The inner problem
partitions the model’s layers across a candidate’s devices to
maximize throughput under memory constraints; existing so-
lutions solve it by dynamic programming (DP) over an ordered
device sequence [9, 10, 11] in O(KL2) time for K devices
arXiv:2611.32881v1  [cs.DC]  24 Nov 2026


--- Page 2 ---
and L layers. Because a candidate’s throughput is unknown
until its inner problem is solved, the exact optimum requires an
inner solver for exponentially many candidates: on a 30-device
fleet with ten device types, exhaustive evaluation takes over
nine hours even with a fast inner solver, and this cost grows
exponentially as fleets grow. Planning time is thus the obstacle
to optimality, and existing planners address it through heuristic
search with no optimality guarantee, namely tabu search [17],
evolutionary search [18], simulated annealing [19], and genetic
algorithms (GA) [9], or by restricting the problem: Parallax [4]
decomposes placement into sequential stages, while the exact
formulations of Helix [6] and Halda [3] solve layer placement
(i.e., the inner problem) rather than replica formation. Using
these inner solvers would also not reduce planning time either,
since each requires solving an integer program for every
candidate, which is still more costly than DP.
Our new solution presented in this paper, SPADE, avoids
both compromises. It solves the outer problem exactly in time
exponential only in the number of device types, which is
typically small in heterogeneous edge fleets, rather than in
the number of devices. Exploiting the interchangeability of
devices of the same type, Spade represents a candidate replica
by its per-type device counts and formulates allocation over the
generated candidates as a bounded multidimensional knapsack,
solved exactly by DP or, when memory is limited, by a
mixed-integer program. SPADE also reduces planning time
by introducing a dominance rule that discards any candidate
whose devices can be decomposed into smaller candidates with
equal or greater aggregate throughput, and skips generating
larger candidates that contain it. Since splitting duplicates
model weights, a decomposition can outperform its parent
only when throughput is latency-bound rather than memory-
bound. We assume that larger candidates containing the parent
inherit this limitation and can therefore be skipped. Across
all instances that we could enumerate exhaustively (Table III),
this assumption eliminated no optimal candidate. Additionally,
because only the head and tail of a replica’s pipeline are
distinct [9], the inner problem admits a closed-form water-
filling solution that reduces complexity from O(KL2) to
O(K). In summary, our contributions are:
• A congestion-aware objective for disaggregated LLM
serving that models the system as a fluid tandem queue
and isolates congestion from Prefill service time (Sec-
tion III-A). On an eight-device CUDA–Metal testbed,
placements selected by this objective reduce worst-case
waiting time by up to 2.44× compared with the state-of-
the-art objectives (Section IV-E).
• A scalable placement solution that combines a type-count
knapsack formulation, dominance pruning, and closed-
form water-filling partitioning (Sections III-B–III-E). On
a synthetic 30-device fleet, dominance pruning evaluates
up to 99.6% fewer candidates than exhaustive enumera-
tion, and Spade reaches the verified optimum in 441 ms,
whereas the state-of-the-art method requires 6855 s and
yields 19.7% higher congestion (Section IV-D).
• An open-source peer-to-peer serving framework built
on llama.cpp. Unlike the star topology used by
llama.cpp and E2LLM, which routes all activations
through a single node, the framework enables fully de-
centralized communication (Section IV-F).
II. RELATED WORK
A. Distributed LLM inference on heterogeneous devices
Partitioning a model across multiple devices is well estab-
lished. PipeEdge and EdgeShard partition transformer layers
under memory constraints [10, 11]; LOIP, Parallax, and Helix
extend placement to heterogeneous deployments with commu-
nication, scheduling, and optimization constraints [5, 4, 6]; and
prima.cpp (Halda) targets consumer hardware through integer-
programming placement and disk offloading [3]. LOIP and
prima.cpp optimize single-pipeline deployments for single-
request metrics such as TPOT and latency, whereas Parallax
and Helix maximize aggregate throughput. However, none of
these systems models congestion explicitly as a placement
objective or assigns distinct Prefill and Decode roles to dif-
ferent replicas. While E2LLM instantiates multiple Prefill and
Decode replicas on heterogeneous edge fleets [9], its objective
couples congestion with Prefill service time. We additionally
find that prima.cpp’s multi-round SSD–CPU–GPU pipeline is
effective only in its CPU execution; GPU execution falls back
to a single round with one microbatch, eliminating the pipeline
and overlap that motivate the design (Section IV).
B. Prefill–decode disaggregation
Prefill–decode disaggregation is now a common practice
in LLM serving. Splitwise separates the two phases onto
dedicated machine pools [13], DistServe jointly optimizes their
placement and parallelism [14], and HexGen-2 extends the
approach to heterogeneous GPU clusters [16]. More recent
work refines resource allocation through workload-aware rout-
ing and analytical provisioning [15, 20]. Hence, we adopt
disaggregation rather than introducing it. The key difference
is that existing systems treat role assignment largely as a pro-
visioning decision, whereas heterogeneous edge fleets contain
devices that differ substantially in compute performance and
memory capacity, precisely the resources stressed by Prefill
and Decode, respectively. Consequently, assigning a device to
a phase becomes part of the placement problem itself.
C. Queueing and contention in LLM serving
As LLM serving systems matured, attention shifted from
execution latency to the congestion that emerges under load.
Analytical models provision Prefill and Decode capacity under
TTFT targets [20], while measurement studies show that
queueing delay and KV-cache transfer dominate tail TTFT
in loaded clusters [15]. Subsequent work addresses conges-
tion through scheduling, including Peace [21] and APEX
[22], but treats device heterogeneity as largely orthogonal to
the optimization. E2LLM extends placement optimization to
heterogeneous edge fleets and allows multiple replicas [9],
yet estimates latency by combining Prefill service time with


--- Page 3 ---
bottleneck-phase congestion. As discussed in Section I, this
couples service costs with queueing effects and can reward
additional Prefill capacity without reducing congestion. Our
work starts from the same edge-serving setting but models
Prefill and Decode as a fluid tandem queue, isolating con-
gestion from service costs and optimizing placement directly
around the resulting queueing behavior.
D. Multi-cluster placement problem
Once multiple LLM replicas can be deployed simultane-
ously, placement becomes a combinatorial problem because
devices must be allocated across replicas. Selecting which
devices form a replica is a clustering problem with an ex-
ponential search space, and ThunderServe explicitly identifies
the problem as NP-hard [17]. Existing systems therefore rely
on heuristic search to navigate that complexity. HexGen forms
asymmetric groups through evolutionary search [18]; HexGen-
2 [16] replaces evolutionary search with spectral partitioning
refined by Kernighan–Lin, evaluates each candidate through a
max-flow formulation that selects per-group parallel strategies
and KV-cache communication paths, and further improves
solutions through max-flow-guided edge swaps. HexGen-3
employs simulated annealing, a metaheuristic optimization
algorithm, to search for a deployment plan [19]. ThunderServe
adopts tabu search [17], while E2LLM uses a GA [9]. These
methods substantially reduce search cost and scale to larger
deployments, but they offer no optimality guarantee.
Exact optimization has also been explored. Helix formulates
placement as a max-flow mixed-integer linear program [6],
while Halda decomposes an integer program over layer assign-
ments [3]. However, these methods optimize layer placement
within a pipeline rather than the higher-level problem of
selecting and composing multiple replicas from a hetero-
geneous fleet. Additionally, the challenge is not expressing
the optimization problem, but evaluating the vast number
of candidate replicas it generates. Before a replica can be
compared with another, its throughput must first be estimated
by solving an inner layer-partitioning problem. Consequently,
the cost of replica evaluation quickly dominates planning time
(see Section IV-D). Reducing this cost is therefore key to
the feasibility and scalability of the planner. Existing work
therefore tends to treat exactness and tractability as competing
objectives. Our approach reconciles the two for the outer prob-
lem. The dominance rule introduced in Section III eliminates
the need to evaluate the overwhelming majority of candidates,
removing the principal computational bottleneck and making
placement optimization tractable at fleet scale.
III. PROPOSED METHOD
Figure 1 provides an overview of SPADE. First, SPADE
constructs list of candidates for the outer problem and solves
inner problem with water-filling formulation (Section III-B).
Additionally, SPADE applies the dominance rule while con-
structing the list to eliminate unpromising candidates and thus
reducing the search space (Section III-D). Finally, it solves the
outer problem (Section III-E) based on the congestion model
of disaggregated Prefill/Decode to determine the placement
that minimizes the modelled congestion (Section III-A).
A. Congestion model for prefill/decode placement
We model a disaggregated deployment consisting of at least
one Prefill replica and one Decoder replica. Every request must
first traverse a Prefill before being forwarded to a Decoder,
making the deployment a two-stage tandem queue rather
than two independent services. Let PS and DS denote the
aggregate Prefill and Decoder throughput of the deployment
in tokens per second, NP the average number of input tokens
per request, ND the average number of generated tokens,
and Ta the average inter-arrival period between requests. The
aggregate throughputs follow directly from the partition plan
described in Section III-B, summed over all replicas assigned
to each phase. We define
tP = NP /PS,
tD = ND/DS
(1)
as the service times of the Prefill and Decoder stages, respec-
tively. Congestion appears in the Prefill stage (CP ) only when
requests arrive faster than the stage can serve them, i.e., when
the prefill time tP exceed the average inter-arrival period.
CP = max(0, tP −Ta) .
(2)
The Decoder stage experiences a different arrival process.
Once Prefill becomes saturated, requests can leave the first
stage no faster than the Prefill service rate. Consequently,
the Decoder does not observe the external arrival period Ta
directly. Instead, requests arrive at intervals
TD = max(Ta, tP ) ,
(3)
which reflects either the original request stream or the throt-
tled output of a saturated Prefill stage. Measuring Decoder
congestion against Ta would therefore count the delay twice.
Decoder congestion CD is instead determined by the excess of
its service time over the period at which work actually arrives:
CD = max(0, tD −TD) .
(4)
Once a queue forms, the delay experienced by later requests
accumulates. Each arriving request inherits the backlog gen-
erated by earlier requests, causing congestion to grow linearly
over the burst. SPADE selects the placement that minimizes
W = CP + CD. The congestion can happen in either a single
phase or both phases. For the former scenarios, allocating
more resources on the congested phase would help. For the
latter scenarios, from Eqs. 2–4, the congestion happens on
both phases when tD > tP > Ta. In this regime, Decoder
is the dominant bottleneck: increasing Decoder throughput
reduces both Decoder congestion and total waiting time,
regardless of congestion in the Prefill stage. Hence, allocating
more resources to Decoder is generally more beneficial than
increasing Prefill capacity.

B. Model partitioning with water-filling
Before a placement can be evaluated, we must determine
how the transformer’s layers are distributed across each replica
and estimate the throughput that replica can sustain. A pipeline
replica is a complete copy of the LLM deployed across a
subset of devices. The assigned devices collectively host all
L transformer layers and execute them as a pipeline-parallel
ring. Device i stores a contiguous block of ℓi layers:
X
i
ℓi = L,
ℓi ≥ℓmin,
(5)
which limits devices assigned to a replica to at most
Kmax =
 L
ℓmin

(6)
Unlike a centralized deployment, positions within a pipeline
sequence are not interchangeable. The head device hosts the
embedding table and the tail device the final normalization and
output projection, making both the fixed memory overhead
ci(r) and fixed stage latency cost αi(r) depend on the role
r ∈{head, mid, tail}. A replica of K devices therefore admits
K(K −1) distinct head–tail assignments [9], each inducing
a different optimal partition. We enumerate these assignments
while treating the intermediate devices as interchangeable.
a) Memory limit: The first constraint on replica through-
put is memory. Every device must store both the weights of
its assigned layers and the key–value cache associated with
all active requests. If a replica serves s concurrent requests,
device i in role r must satisfy
ℓiw + s ℓiκ + ci(r) ≤Mi,
(7)
where w denotes the per-layer weight footprint, κ the per-layer
key–value footprint per request, and Mi the usable memory
capacity of the device. Eq. (7) reveals an immediate tradeoff.
Assigning more layers to a device increases both its weight
footprint and its share of the key–value cache, reducing the
number of concurrent requests that the device can support.
Rearranging the constraint gives
s ≤(Mi −ci(r))/ℓi −w
κ
,
which is the maximum requests device i can accommodate.
Because this quantity decreases as ℓi grows, the replica’s
capacity is ultimately determined by the most memory-
constrained device. Any imbalance in layer assignment there-
fore leaves memory unused on some devices while constrain-
ing concurrency on others.
The optimal partition avoids this imbalance by equalizing
the memory-limited slot count (smem) across devices. This
yields a water-filling solution in which ℓi ∝Mi −ci(r),
so devices with larger effective memory budgets receive pro-
portionally more layers. Combining this relationship with the
constraint P

replica after accounting for role-specific overheads. Eq. 8
characterizes a memory-capacity bound rather than the par-
tition ultimately selected by the planner. It answers a simpler
question: how many requests could the replica support if
memory were the only limiting resource? Section III-D uses
this bound to compare replicas and identify candidates that
can be safely discarded.
b) Concurrency limit: Memory determines how many
requests a replica could accommodate, but the maximum
concurrency is ultimately set by throughput. As concurrency
increases, the throughput available to each request falls be-
cause the available resources are shared among more in-
flight requests. We therefore admit requests only while per-
request throughput remains above the deployment target τ
(i.e., minimum tokens per second). Let ρ(S, s) denote the per-
request throughput achieved by candidate S when serving s
requests. Hence the largest admissible concurrency is
scon = max{s : ρ(S, s) ≥τ},
(9)
Finally, the achievable serving request is therefore governed
by whichever constraint becomes active first. A replica may
exhaust its memory before throughput falls below τ, or reach
the throughput limit while memory remains available. In either


--- Page 5 ---
case, the active constraint determines the concurrency level
used when evaluating the replica. The overall throughput of a
candidate S is

(10)
c) The partition: Existing planners [10, 11] obtain a
layer assignment by DP over an ordered device sequence. We
observe that the assignment admits a much simpler structure.
Throughput is determined by the slowest pipeline stage, so
any assignment that leaves one device slower than the others
can be improved by shifting layers away from that device. At
the optimum, therefore, all stages progress at the same rate.
We model the execution time of device i as an affine
function of the number of layers assigned to it
ti(ℓ) = αi(ri) + βiℓi,
(11)
where αi(r) captures the fixed per-token latency cost asso-
ciated with role ri and βi is the measured per-layer latency
cost of the device. Because ti increases monotonically with
ℓi, maximizing throughput is equivalent to minimizing the
slowest stage, which occurs when all devices attain a com-
mon stage time t⋆. The layer assignments therefore satisfy
ℓi = (t⋆−αi(r))/(βi). Combining this condition with the
conservation constraint P
i ℓi = L yields
L =

(12)
The partition therefore follows in closed form. Once t⋆is
known, the layer counts are computed directly, after which
they are rounded and repaired to satisfy both ℓmin and the
memory constraint of Eq. 7. Because the head and tail devices
incur different fixed costs, both αi(r) and ci(r) depend on the
selected role assignment. Eq. 12 is therefore solved once for
each of the K(K −1) admissible head–tail assignments, and
the assignment achieving the highest throughput is retained.
d) Complexity: Water filling evaluates Eq. 12 in O(K)
time for a replica of K devices. DP instead requires O(KL2)
time by considering every layer boundary at every device.
Enumerating the K(K −1) head–tail assignments yields
O(K3) under water filling versus O(K3L2) under DP, an L2
advantage that is significant in practice because L ≫K.
C. A type-count representation for replicas
The observation that makes the outer search space manage-
able is that devices of the same hardware type are interchange-
able. Devices sharing a type have the same memory budget and
the same measured performance profile, so any two replicas
that draw the same number of devices from each type receive
identical throughput estimates and therefore identical scores.
The planner need not distinguish individual devices.
Since a replica is fully characterized by the devices assigned
to it, we represent a candidate device allocation for a replica
using a type-count vector c = (c1, . . . , ct) where ct denotes
the number of devices drawn from type t and 0 ≤ct ≤mt,
with mt the number of available devices of that type. The
search therefore moves from individual device subsets to
configurations of device types. This representation reduces the
number of candidates from the 2N −1 non-empty subsets of
an N-device fleet to
T
Y
t=1
(mt + 1) −1,
(13)
which counts the non-empty type-count vectors. Candidates
containing more than Kmax devices are infeasible by con-
struction and are discarded without evaluation.
D. Search space pruning
Even after the reduction of Eq. 13, the search space remains
large. We therefore identify dominated candidates. A candidate
is dominated if it can be decomposed into valid sub-candidates
whose combined throughput is no smaller than its own. Such
a candidate can be discarded. Dominance is evaluated recur-
sively from previously generated candidates, avoiding explicit
enumeration of all decompositions.
a) Discarding a dominated candidate is lossless.: Re-
placing a dominated candidate with the feasible replicas of its
best decomposition preserves feasibility because both consume
the same fleet resources. Since the decomposition provides
at least as much aggregate throughput in the candidate’s
role, and the objective depends only on those aggregates, the
replacement cannot increase congestion. An optimal placement
therefore exists that excludes the dominated candidate, allow-
ing it to be removed without loss of optimality. This argument
does not extend to per-request metrics such as TPOT.
b) A dominated candidate is limited by latency, not by
memory: Dominance alone saves search rather than evalua-
tion, since a candidate’s throughput must already be known
before domination can be tested. The key observation is a
memory ledger. Every replica stores a complete copy of the
model weights, so decomposing a device set a into b+c pays
the weight cost twice. From Eq. 8,
smem(b) + smem(c) = smem(a) −w/κ.
(14)
A decomposition therefore begins with fewer slots than
the candidate it replaces. If it nevertheless achieves higher
throughput, the gain must come from a higher service rate
rather than additional memory. Dominance thus identifies can-
didates whose throughput is limited by latency, not memory.
c) Extending the rule to larger candidates.: Discarding
a dominated candidate saves search but not evaluation, since
its value must already be known to test the domination. The
real benefit arises if dominance also propagates to larger
candidates. Let a set of device d be added to a, and suppose
the same device is instead placed within one part of its
dominating decomposition. A dominated candidate has already
grown beyond the point where additional memory translates
into useful concurrency. Adding another device therefore con-
tributes mainly an extra stage, whereas a smaller replica can
still convert the added memory into throughput. The additional
device is consequently worth more in the decomposition than
in the already dominated candidate.


--- Page 6 ---
A general proof is significantly complicated by role-
dependent costs, heterogeneous devices, and the fact that a
decomposition and its parent candidate need not operate in
the same regime. We therefore adopt this extension as an
assumption used during candidate generation rather than as
a theorem. While violating the assumption may invalidate
the optimality guarantee, our experimental results suggest
that the resulting planner still produces high-quality solutions
while significantly reducing solving time compared to exist-
ing methods. The assumption affects only which candidates
are generated. The outer solver remains exact over those
candidates, and removing a dominated candidate is itself
lossless (see Section III-D.a). The extension simply avoids
generating descendants of candidates that have already been
shown uncompetitive. In Section IV, we show that exhaus-
tive enumeration and dominance pruning produce identical
survivor sets, Pareto frontiers, and final placements whenever
exhaustive comparison is affordable.
E. Placement method
The surviving candidates form a bounded multidimen-
sional knapsack: choose how many replicas of each surviving
type-count vector to instantiate, and in which role, subject
to the available devices of each type. Since the objective W
depends on a placement only through (PS, DS), the prob-
lem reduces to enumerating the Pareto frontier of achievable
throughput pairs and evaluating W on that frontier.
We consider two exact formulations. The first is a multi-
dimension knapsack DP [23] whose states are device-
consumption vectors u ≤(m1, . . . , mT ). Each transition adds
one surviving candidate in one of the two roles and updates
the reachable (PS, DS) frontier. This DP is different from
layer-partitioning DP. The second is a mixed-integer program
over replica counts xr
c:
min
W(PS, DS)
s.t.
X
r
X
c
xr
c ct ≤mt
∀t,
(15)
PS =
X
c
xP
c γP (c),
DS =
X

xD
c γD(c). (16)
The two formulations trade time for memory. The DP is
faster because it constructs the entire Pareto frontier in a single
forward pass and remains exact by construction. However, its
speed comes at the cost of working memory: the state table
spans Q
t(mt + 1) entries and therefore grows exponentially
with the number of device types. This is often acceptable for
heterogeneous edge fleets, where the number of types is small
even when the number of devices is large, but it eventually
becomes the limiting resource.
The mixed-integer program makes the opposite tradeoff.
By avoiding the state table altogether, its memory footprint
remains modest as the type count grows. However, the cost
is runtime: the Pareto frontier must be recovered through
repeated solves, each corresponding to a different scalarization
of (PS, DS). We therefore use the DP whenever its state space
fits comfortably in memory and fall back to the mixed-integer

IV. EVALUATION AND DISCUSSION
Our evaluation proceeds in four steps. We first investigate
which existing solutions can serve as meaningful baselines
in our deployment regime and explain why others cannot
be compared directly (Section IV-B). We then validate the
per-replica cost model on which dominance pruning depends
(Section IV-C). Next, we compare SPADE with placement
planners of the selected baselines in both solution quality and
planning time, isolating the contribution of the dominance
rule (Section IV-D). Finally, we study how the queueing-
aware objective affects the resulting deployment as the model,
workload, arrival rate, and fleet size vary (Section IV-E).
A. Experiment setup
Our testbed consists of eight devices spanning five hard-
ware types and connected through a local-area network
(Table I). To emulate a resource-constrained edge device,
we limit the DGX Spark to 12 GB of VRAM. Following
E2LLM [9], we deploy our testbed on a Local Area Net-
work (about 900Mbps) to reduce the affect of transmit-
ting time on pipeline paralellism. We evaluate two con-
trasting models: DeepSeek R1 Distill Qwen 14B Q6 K and
Qwen3-30B-A3B-Q4 K M, referred to as DeepSeekR1 and
Qwen3MoE. DeepSeekR1 stores 11.3 GB of weights but ac-
tivates all 14B parameters through dense FFNs [24], whereas
Qwen3MoE stores 17.3 GB of weights but activates only about
3B parameters through a Mixture-of-Experts architecture [25].
The two models therefore represent latency- and memory-
constrained deployment regimes, respectively. Workloads are
drawn from the LZByteDance [26] and IELTS [27] datasets
which together represent different NP /ND ratios as in Table
II. Moreover, the service target is set to τ = 15 tokens/s
per request, doubling the average human reading speed [28].
Request inter-arrival times follow a normal distribution with
mean Ta and standard deviation σ = 0.1Ta, truncated at zero.
B. Baselines chosen
Systems that cannot execute in this regime. Several
published systems cannot be evaluated directly on our testbed.


--- Page 7 ---
PipeEdge targets encoder models without a key–value cache,
and its partitioning cost model does not extend to autoregres-
sive decoding. In addition, HexGen, HexGen-2, HexGen-3,
ThunderServe and Splitwise depend on CUDA and NCCL,
which are unavailable on Mac devices and edge fleet on LAN.
We therefore cannot compare against their full implementa-
tions. Instead, we compare with their planners and objectives,
as mentioned below.
Objectives evaluated inside our planner. Placement ob-
jectives and placement searches solve different problems, and
evaluating them together confounds the effect of one with
the other. Therefore, within our own planner, we evaluate the
following placement objectives: finishing time (from HexGen
[18] - FT), role-pinned disaggregation (from Splitwise [13],
called adapted Splitwise - SPW), and the congestion objec-
tive in E2LLM. For SPW, we derive a role-pinned policy
from the deployment choices reported in Splitwise, where the
higher-throughput resources are consistently assigned to Prefill
and lower-throughput to Decode. Differences in the resulting
placements can then be attributed to the objective alone rather
than to differences in the implementation. These experiments
should therefore be understood as objective-level ablations.
Search methods compared directly. To isolate the effect of
the search algorithm, we compare three alternatives: a genetic
algorithm (GA) combined with our water-filling partitioner,
a GA paired with the layer-partitioning DP used in E2LLM
[9], and the tabu search employed by ThunderServe [17]. All
methods are run with the parameters reported by their authors;
no search-specific tuning was performed for our fleet.
Moreover, prima.cpp [3] is the closest published system
that executes on our hardware. Halda as its planner relies
on pipeline-ring parallelism (PRP), in which weight transfers
overlap computation through multiple execution rounds (k >
1). Rebuilding prima.cpp with a GPU backend and reproducing
Halda’s parameter selection on our devices showed that this
mechanism never activates in our setting. For PRP to hide
storage latency, the device compute rate must satisfy
rate ≤(N −1) I disk bw
(17)
where I is the model arithmetic intensity and disk bw the
storage bandwidth. For the Llama-3-70B Q4 K M model
used in their original evaluation, the bound is approxi-
mately 60 GFLOPS per device on a four-device deployment
(I = 3.32, SSD disk bw = 6GB/s), whereas the slow-
est CPU in our fleet reaches 66.4 GFLOPS and the fastest
GPU 87,207 GFLOPS, measured by their tool. The overlap
condition is therefore violated throughout our fleet, causing
prima.cpp to fall back to a single-round pipeline with only
one microbatch in flight. While still pipeline-parallel, this
execution regime no longer benefits from pipeline filling
or weight-fetch overlap, both of which are fundamental to
efficient pipeline parallelism [11, 10, 12]. Since prima.cpp
operates in a substantially inefficient regime from the studies in
this work, we do not include it in the end-to-end comparison.
C. Pipeline parallelism performance prediction
The dominance rule prunes candidates without evaluating
them, and the outer solver ranks placements that it never needs
to execute. Both therefore depend on the accuracy of the per-
replica cost model. Following E2LLM [9] and EdgeShard [11],
we model a fully populated pipeline by its bottleneck stage:
TPOT = Tslowest × Nstage.
(18)
To validate Eq. 18, we sampled deployments from our fleet,
including non-optimal placements.When evaluated on mea-
sured stage times and performance, Eq. 18 predicts throughput
with less than 0.5% error across all deployments, confirming
that throughput is well explained by the bottleneck-stage
model. We next combine the stage-time predictor (Eq. 11)
with the bottleneck-stage model of Eq. 18 to estimate replica
throughput. The predictions achieve an average error of 5.22%
across all deployments. Figure 2 shows the error distribution.
D. Planner comparison
Table III evaluates the effect of dominance pruning on
synthetic 30 devices derived from our 8-device testbed by
replicating the observed hardware types with varying memory
capacities and compute throughput. The evaluations are based
on the water-filling method. Without pruning, every candidate
must be generated and priced before the outer solver runs.
With pruning, only candidates that survive the dominance test
are evaluated. The savings are substantial. At T = 5 device
types, exhaustive generation evaluates 16554 candidates and
requires 153 s for the whole process, whereas the pruned gen-
erator evaluates only 238 candidates and completes everything
in 0.44 s, a 347× reduction in runtime. At T = 10, the gap
widens from 35 252 s (more than nine hours) to 11.24 s, a
3 136× reduction, with only 3 710 of 1 045 682 candidates
ever evaluated. The advantage grows with the number of
device types, which is precisely the dimension along which the
search space grows exponentially. These savings come with no
observable loss in solution quality because at both scales, ex-
haustive and pruned generation produce identical survivor sets,
identical Pareto frontiers, and the same final placement. This is
the empirical validation referred to in Section III-D: although
the extension rule is not proven lossless in general, exhaustive
enumeration confirms that it preserves all candidates required
to recover the optimum.
a) Search methods: Table IV compares the placement
searches on two rosters: the physical fleet and a 30-device
roster constructed by replicating the measured device types.

--- Page 8 ---
On the physical fleet, all methods reach the same optimum
and differ only in planning cost. Our planner completes in
109.4 ms, compared with 384.4 ms for tabu search, 548.0 ms
for the genetic algorithm with water-filling partitioning, and
8 257 ms for the genetic algorithm paired with the layer-
partitioning DP. At eight devices the search space is suffi-
ciently small that solution quality is no longer discriminative,
and we report this rather than selecting only the larger instance.
The picture changes at 30 devices. Our planner reaches the
verified optimum in 441.3 ms. The mixed-integer formulation
also recovers the optimum when the weight grid is sufficiently
fine, requiring 31 ms per Pareto point (PS, DS). Recovering
the full frontier therefore takes 11.3 s, roughly 25.6× longer
than the DP. This asymmetry is structural rather than an
implementation artifact: the DP recovers the entire frontier in a
single backward pass, whereas the MILP must be solved sep-
arately for each Pareto point. The heuristic methods separate
both in runtime and solution quality. The GA yields 18.8%
higher congestion after 230.7 s; replacing water filling with
the layer-partitioning DP increases runtime to 6 855 s while
still yielding 19.7% higher congestion. Tabu search completes
in 13.4 s but yields 20.4% higher congestion. Interestingly,
varying the parameters of tabu search does not materially
reduce the gap, and likewise for GA, a typical behavior
of heuristic searches that provide no optimality guarantees.
Optimal planning is hence tractable at this scale: SPADE
reaches the optimum in milliseconds, while the heuristic ones
are either slower, less accurate, or both.
b) Memory: The two exact formulations exhibit the
tradeoff predicted in Section III-E. The multidimensional-
knapsack DP is the faster solver, but its dense state table
grows exponentially with the number of device types. On
our largest roster, it requires 4.75 GB of memory. The mixed-
integer program makes the opposite tradeoff, reproducing the
same frontier using only 122 MB while requiring longer solve
times. With larger device types, for example 50 devices in 20
types, the DP no longer fits in memory, leaving the mixed-
integer formulation as the only practical exact solver.
E. Placement objective comparison
We now hold the planner fixed and vary only the objective,
so any differences in the resulting deployments are attributable
to the objective itself. Following E2LLM, we evaluate them
across four dimensions: model architecture, arrival rate, work-
load, and fleet scale. Table V summarizes results of the four
objectives across all evaluation dimensions. In Tables VI, VII,
and VIII, R denotes the replica role (P = Prefill, D = Decode),
Sl. the total slot count, and G-C the numbers of GPU and

CPU layers assigned to the replica. The first device is always
the head and the last device is always the tail. For role-
pinned placement (SPW), we do not apply dominance pruning
because the two techniques interact poorly. It should be noted
that in Table V, PS and DS are measured on average. Hence,
even with the same deployment plan, the average performance
may be different depending on the system saturation level.
a) Model change: We first vary the model while hold-
ing the fleet (eight devices), workload (LZByteDance), and
arrival period (100 ms) fixed. Our congestion objective out-
performs all baselines on both models, but the magnitude
of the improvement depends strongly on the model architec-
ture. On Qwen3MoE, the maximum waiting times produced
by FT, E2LLM, and Splitwise are only 4.7%, 4.7%, and
14.2% higher than SPADE, respectively (Table V). Although
these differences appear modest, waiting time accumulates
quadratically with the request count, causing small per-request
discrepancies to translate into substantially different backlog
growth under sustained load. The gap becomes much larger
on DeepSeekR1, where FT, E2LLM, and Splitwise incur
maximum waiting times that are 2.44×, 2.44×, and 3.13× as
long as SPADE, respectively. The contrast reflects the different
operating regimes of the two models. Qwen3MoE activates
only a small fraction of its parameters per token, allowing
it to sustain a relatively high service rate. As concurrency
increases, the deployment continues admitting requests until
memory capacity becomes the limiting factor, as shown in
column DS of Table V. DeepSeekR1, in contrast, activates all
model parameters through dense feed-forward networks, re-
sulting in a substantially lower service rate. Consequently, the
throughput target is reached before memory is exhausted (Eq.
8, 9 and 10), making the deployment limited by latency, rather
than memory. Objectives that ignore phase-specific congestion
are therefore penalized more severely on DeepSeekR1.
b) Workload change: Holding the model at Qwen3MoE,
the fleet at eight devices, and the arrival period at 100 ms
fixed, we switch the workload from IELTS to LZByteDance
(see Table VII). This changes the Prefill-to-Decode token
ratio from 1.17 to 0.77, crossing the point at which Decode
becomes more demanding than Prefill. A placement strategy
that fixes the phase split cannot naturally adapt to this shift;
our congestion objective does. On IELTS, SPADE uses a single
Apple M2 Max for Prefill and dedicates 25 slots to Decode. On
LZByteDance, it reconfigures the deployment by increasing
the Decode pool to 27 slots. Hence, SPADE trades excess
Prefill capacity for greater Decode concurrency. Although the
per-request decode rate is lower than under FT (28.9 vs 31.3
tokens/s), the larger pool raises aggregate decode throughput

by about 31% (27 vs 19 slots), thus reducing congestion.
In contrast, FT and E2LLM objectives retain the same three
Prefill devices across both workloads and adjust only the
layer partition boundaries, by a single layer. E2LLM behaves
similarly because its objective still includes the Prefill service-
time term. Although the workload changes substantially, the
reduction in Prefill service time remains large enough to
outweigh the benefit of reallocating devices across phases,
so the optimizer never leaves the original placement. The
workload change nevertheless affects the underlying execution
characteristics. Interestingly, PS reduces whereas DS increases
when changing from IELTS to LZByteDance dataset. Because
Transformer inference relies on self-attention, the cost of a
layer grows with the number of positions already stored in
the KV cache. IELTS and LZByteDance therefore induce
different execution depths, reflected in their different input and
output token counts, and consequently different stage time.
The optimal balance between Prefill and Decode is therefore
not the same across the two workloads.

deployment. Because the search space is discrete, changing
a placement requires replacing an entire replica composition
rather than making an incremental adjustment. The workload
shift is sufficient to alter the objective values, but not sufficient
to move the solution into a different basin of the search space.
Consequently, FT and E2LLM select the same plan and differ
only in the value they assign to it. Adapted Splitwise is even
more rigid, keeping the RTX5070 in Prefill for both workloads
because its rule always assigns the highest-throughput replica
to Prefill regardless of workload characteristics.
c) Arrival rate change: Holding the model, workload,
and fleet fixed at Qwen3MoE, LZByteDance, and eight de-
vices, respectively, we vary the arrival period from 100 ms
to 3000 ms (Table VIII). This is the only configuration that
transitions from overload to under-load, with the crossover
occurring between 1 s and 2 s. Within the overloaded regime,
placements remain unchanged: SPADE and E2LLM retain their
deployments up to 1000 ms and converge to the same place-
ment at 3000 ms, whereas finishing time and adapted Splitwise
keep the same deployment throughout. The throughput gains
remain visible after the transition. At 3000 ms, the per-request


--- Page 10 ---
decode rate reaches 59.0 tokens/s under SPADE and E2LLM,
compared with 46.8 tokens/s under finishing time and 33.1
tokens/s under adapted Splitwise. Once excess Prefill capacity
no longer reduces congestion, SPADE reallocates resources
toward Decode. Combined with its higher decode throughput
and larger decode pool at saturation, this allows idle capacity
to be converted into higher per-request throughput even after
waiting time reaches zero. The most interesting observation
is that SPADE and E2LLM eventually converge to the same
deployment. Once the offered load falls sufficiently below ca-
pacity, additional Prefill resources no longer reduce queueing
delay, and both objectives therefore shift resources toward
Decode despite being derived from different formulations.
One exception appears at an arrival period of 3000 ms,
where SPADE still exhibits approximately 7 s of maximum
waiting time (Table V). The log from experiments showed
that measured Prefill throughput was up to 30% lower than
predicted, causing residual congestion. The discrepancy arises
because the planner represents a workload using a representa-
tive sequence length rather than the full request-length distri-
bution. Since latency scales nonlinearly with sequence length,
the throughput evaluated at the representative length generally
differs from the average throughput over the workload. This
approximation substantially reduces planning complexity and
is consistent with the workload abstractions commonly used in
prior deployment planners [13, 17, 19]. Importantly, this effect
is confined to Prefill. Decode throughput remains accurately
predicted. The same over-prediction exists in the overloaded
configurations, but there the predicted bottleneck matches the
measured one, so it changes only the magnitude of congestion.
At 3000 ms the model predicts W = 0, yet measurements
show residual Prefill congestion. We also observe small dif-
ferences in Prefill throughput for SPW despite the same
Prefill. These differences are likely caused by device power
management under varying idle times. We do not analyze this
further, as it concerns runtime behavior rather than placement.
d) Scalability: We evaluate nested rosters of four, six,
and eight devices so that fleet size is never confounded
with fleet composition. The four-device fleet consists of one
Type.1, one Type.2, and two Type.4 devices; the 6-device fleet
additionally includes one Type.3 and one Type.5 device; and
the 8-device fleet uses all devices. Across all fleet sizes, SPADE
consistently achieves the lowest maximum waiting time. The
advantage is most pronounced on the smallest fleet, where
the finishing-time and E2LLM objectives incur 17% longer
maximum waiting times and adapted Splitwise incurs 160%
longer maximum waiting times relative to SPADE.
F. Framework comparison
SPADE is built on llama.cpp but replaces the original
star-topology communication with a peer-to-peer pipeline. We
therefore compare against both the original llama.cpp im-
plementation and E2LLM, which also adopts a star topology.
With three devices and nine slots (Type.1, Type.5, Type.2),
SPADE achieves 37.13 tokens/s, compared with 25.23 tokens/s
for E2LLM and 12.69 tokens/s for llama.cpp. At this

scale, E2LLM benefits from distributed pipeline execution,
whereas the original llama.cpp cannot perform networked
pipeline parallelism. The picture changes as the pipeline
grows. With six devices and 18 slots (first decoder replica,
Table VIII.d), SPADE sustains 23.92 tokens/s, whereas E2LLM
and llama.cpp achieve only 5.02 and 6.29 tokens/s, respec-
tively. The reason is communication contention. In E2LLM,
every stage exchanges activations through a central node,
forcing multiple pipeline stages to compete for the same
uplink and downlink bandwidth. As additional stages are
added, communication becomes the dominant bottleneck and
eventually outweighs the benefit of pipeline parallelism itself,
causing E2LLM to perform even worse than the original
llama.cpp. In contrast, the P2P ring distributes traffic across
devices and avoids concentrating on a single node, allowing
throughput to scale more gracefully with pipeline depth.
G. Limitations of SPADE
As mentioned, SPADE predicts Prefill throughput accurately
for individual operating points, but the throughput of an aver-
age request is not necessarily equal to the average throughput
across requests. Consequently, workloads represented only by
average input lengths can introduce high prediction error when
request lengths exhibit high variance. In addition, SPADE
targets static deployment planning. The optimizer assumes a
fixed workload characterization, arrival rate, and fleet compo-
sition during planning. Dynamic adaptations such as online
role reassignment, replica migration, or re-optimization under
changing arrival rates and request sizes are complementary to
our work and remain future directions. Finally, the extension
of dominance to descendant replicas is supported empirically
rather than proven lossless in general. Exhaustive ones produce
identical survivor sets, Pareto frontiers, and final placements
wherever verification remains computationally affordable, but
a general proof remains open.


--- Page 11 ---
V. CONCLUSION
We presented SPADE, a tractable and scalable placement
planner for heterogeneous edge fleets. SPADE models disag-
gregated Prefill/Decode serving as a queueing system and opti-
mizes congestion directly. To make the optimization tractable,
it combines pruning with a water-filling formulation for layer
partitioning, pruning up to 99.6% of candidates while pre-
serving the same survivor set as exhaustive ones. Combined
with water filling, SPADE reaches the verified optimum in
hundreds of milliseconds on a 30-device fleet, whereas heuris-
tic searches remain substantially below optimum even after
seconds to hours of execution. These results suggest that
optimal queueing-aware placement for heterogeneous edge
serving is tractable at fleet scale.
